newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB shares dip after reports of prosecutors' raid.
newsitem.headline: DKB shares dip after reports of prosecutors' raid.

text.p: Shares in Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) slid in early Tokyo trading on Tuesday following Japanese media reports that Tokyo prosecutors had entered the bank's headquarters in what appeared to be a raid.
As of 0011 GMT, the shares were down 60 yen at 1,410 yen, making the Japanese bank the biggest percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Turnover was 1.13 million.
Jiji news agency reported that prosecutors were seen entering the headquarters of DKB in what appeared to be a raid.

A DKB spokesman said some officers from the Tokyo Prosecutors' Office had entered through the main reception area of the headquarters, but they could not confirm whether the purpose was to raid the premises.

DKB officials have remained tight-lipped on media reports that the bank is being questioned by prosecutors over its questionable loans to a racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities Co Ltd scandal.

The daily Mainichi Shimbun reported on Sunday that executives at DKB had been questioned by prosecutors in connection with questionable loans to a principal figure in the Nomura scandal, "sokaiya" Ryuichi Koike.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
The Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

On Monday, the Mainichi also reported that Ryuichi Koike owned about 20,000 DKB shares under various assumed names, and often attended DKB's annual shareholders' meeting as a "friendly sokaiya". Typically, "friendly sokaiya" use their influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts at annual shareholders' meetings.
